https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/educa.text: Education Covid impacts and enhanced grades: five takeaways from 2026 Leaving Cert results Friday’s results, in the aggregate, are close to those awarded in 2020 IT Explains: How does Leaving Cert results day work? Video: Bryan O'Brien Editor: Eoin Ronayne Brian Mooney Fri Aug 21 2026 - 06:01 • 4 MIN READ M ore than 70,000 students will log on to their Leaving Certificate portal on Friday morning to receive the results of their examinations. Some 65,326 students took the traditional Leaving Cert, 4,779 sat the Leaving Cert Applied and 306 sat the level-one and level-two learning programmes. These numbers represent a 15 per cent increase over the past two years, bringing us to the highest participation ever in the 100-year history of the exam. Here are five key takeaways from the 2026 Leaving Cert results. 1) The consequences of Covid are still with us The fallout from the calculated grades awarded during Covid-19 is still playing out as the Government gradually unwinds the adjustments that saw grades increase by an average of 4.6 per cent in 2020 and a further 2.4 per cent in 2021. READ MORE Have your say: Has your child refused to go to school? Most primary and secondary students refused to go to school at least once last year Aoibhinn Ní Shúilleabháin quits Leaving Cert maths reform group after concerns ‘ignored’ ‘I’m officially retiring from my primary school - and I’ve had a good run’ The results on Friday, in the aggregate, are close to those awarded in 2020, which means the students receiving their results on Friday morning are securing grades equal to those awarded in September 2020 by teachers through the calculated grades process. Effectively, through adjusting the enhancement downwards over the past two years, the State Exams Commission ( SEC ) has removed the 2.4 additional increase in grades awarded in 2021, which was retained for a further three years, 2022-2024. 2) No further enhancement beyond 2027 The SEC has indicated it will repeat this process of unwinding the enhanced grades further in 2027, which, if equivalent to the past two years, will see a further 1.2 per cent reduction. There will be no further enhancement of grades in 2028, which will mean the students sitting the exams will, on first observation, experience a 3.4 per cent drop relating to 2027. The SEC has indicated that student performance has improved by an average of 2 per cent since 2019 and that it is therefore not attempting to bring students back to 2019 grade levels. Effectively, this means that by not enhancing grades in 2028 and allowing for a 2 per cent improvement in performance, the class of 2028 will be, on average, 1.2 per cent lower than 2027 and 2.4 per cent lower than those receiving their results on Friday. 3) Cost of doing the exam in 2026 will be about 12 CAO points In 2024, following the enhancement process, 68 per cent of grades were adjusted upwards. In 2025, following the first adjustment downwards, the percentage of grades enhanced dropped to 52.4 per cent. In 2026, this number has fallen farther, to 35.5 per cent. Because students at the higher end of performance get a lower level of enhancement, given that they already have numerous H1s, we cannot be specific about the effect of this process on additional CAO points secured by applicants. We can say that, from 2021-2024, Leaving Cert students got an extra grade in four to five of their subjects; in 2025, three to four of their subjects; and Friday in two to three of their subjects. Effectively, a student in the class of 2026 will have, on average, 12 fewer CAO points than an equivalent student who sat the exam in 2025, and 24 fewer CAO points than an equivalent student who sat the exam in 2021-2024. 4) Winding down the enhanced grades is tricky The differentials are significant because 55,357 of this year’s Leaving Cert cohort have applied for a college place through the CAO, but 20,527 applicants have sat the exam in previous years, mainly in the past two to three years. Where competition for places is at its fiercest, this differential in points secured by students who got the same marks from their correcting examiner will favour those holding awards from previous years. 5) Some subjects are growing in popularity Given the overall increase in the number of students taking the Leaving Cert in the past two years, one would expect an average increase of 7-8 per cent. Subjects that exceeded this significantly are PE, which increased by 26 per cent; Technology, 21 per cent; Polish, 23 per cent; Ukrainian, 18 per cent; and Mandarin Chinese by a whopping 47 per cent. Many schools in certain postal districts of Dublin have experienced a very significant growth in their Chinese student population in recent years. Ireland’s education system is obviously held in high regard internationally. History teachers fought a battle following the reforms to the junior cycle to retain their subject as core. They will be more than pleased to see that 10 per cent more students took history in 2026 than previously. Post Script Given the population bulge, which is manifesting itself at senior cycle level, the outcome of the 2026 Leaving Cert will only be measured once we see how the 70,411 individuals involved progress over the coming weeks. Thankfully, the options on offer to these school leavers have never been more comprehensive. More than 40,000 of them will secure places through the CAO next Wednesday. Many thousands more will start post-Leaving Cert courses in local further education colleges, and others will secure places on the new tertiary degree options. Meanwhile, several thousand will accept offers in Northern Ireland, the UK and, in growing numbers, EU universities. Outside the education system, many thousands will seek and secure apprenticeships in the 80-plus options now available across all sectors of the economy. Photo / 123rf Millions suffer, but spinal problems can be worsened by quick fixes. Here are the expert-approved remedies to try instead. It begins as a niggle when you bend down to tie your shoelaces. Before long, it’s an ache that dictates how you sit, stand, walk and even sleep. It’s tempting to try to banish the misery of this debilitating pain with a variety of quick fixes. But some of the remedies we commonly reach for may be doing little to help – and in some cases, they may even make it worse. “Most people get back pain at some point, and most of us don’t know the best way to manage it,” says Nell Mead, a physiotherapist and author of How To Be Your Own Physio . “We fall back on the things we’ve heard might help, but often, even if they do help for a day or two, we end up back where we began.” Here are some of the most common mistakes people make when treating back pain – and what to do instead. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Staying in bed until the pain goes away When back pain hits, the natural instinct – in line with old medical advice – is to stop moving. But spending days lying down could delay your recovery. Research shows that staying active can lead to better pain relief and a quicker return to normal activities. A 2024 review by the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies concluded that prolonged bed rest can result in joint stiffness, muscle wasting and loss of bone density. When your back hurts, “your nervous system turns the protection up by tightening the muscles around the area,” says Mead. “The way you persuade it to stand down is by showing it, gently and repeatedly, that movement is safe.” Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Ten minutes of walking twice a day is “a perfectly respectable place to start”, she says. “Most people find they can manage a bit more by the end of the week.” The landmark WalkBack trial, led by Australian researchers and published in The Lancet, found that walking three times a week had a “profound impact” on people who had experienced lower back pain within the previous six months, almost halving the risk of recurrence. Taking the wrong painkillers Anti-inflammatory painkillers are more useful for treating back pain. Photo / DepositPhotos Paracetamol alone is not recommended for back pain. The UK NHS specifically advises against using it as a standalone treatment, and a major review of evidence found that it was no better than placebo for acute low back pain, with no meaningful improvement in pain, disability, quality of life or sleep. Dr Lianne Wood, an associate professor and spinal physiotherapy researcher at the University of Exeter, says anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are more useful for treating this type of pain. “They appear to have much more effect than paracetamol on acute back pain, particularly in the early stages,” she says. And there may be some benefit in taking them alongside paracetamol. Research has found that combining paracetamol with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen may cause a small additional reduction in immediate-term pain, compared with the NSAID alone. NSAIDs should not be used long term without medical advice, as they can cause gastrointestinal, kidney and cardiovascular problems. Stronger opioids should only be considered for acute pain when an NSAID is not suitable, has not been tolerated or has not worked. They are highly addictive, however. “People would rather take something for their pain, as opposed to doing something for their pain,” says Dr Wood. But the advice with any medication is to take the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. Using a back brace, support belt or posture-correcting insoles The idea of giving your back added support with a brace or belt can feel reassuring, but while these may provide some short-term relief for some, experts generally discourage their long-term use. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “Belts and corsets tend to reduce your muscle activity,” says Dr Wood. “In the short term, it might make your back feel better because you’re reducing any muscle spasms. But in the long term, you’re becoming reliant on it, and very often people then don’t feel safe to move without it.” This can potentially alter how the muscles work, with some becoming underactive and others overactive. Mead recommends belts to patients on occasion, but says: “I’d treat one as scaffolding, with a plan to remove it once your muscles can take over.” Corrective insoles for shoes are also not advised. “The evidence behind off-the-shelf posture-correcting insoles is thin,” says Mead. Hoping massage or manipulation will fix the problem In a recent review of 301 trials, spinal manipulation by a chiropractor, osteopath or physiotherapist was one of just six non-surgical treatments out of 56 that were found to have a significant effect on pain. But Mead says that while this type of treatment can alleviate pain temporarily, it’s vital to try to work out what’s causing the pain. “The place a body hurts and the place a body is struggling are often not the same – and often the lower back has just run out of capacity to compensate for a problem in another area of the body, such as a stiff hip, a foot that rolls inwards or a ribcage that won’t rotate,” she says. “I go looking for that first and treat the back second.” The aim is to use hands-on treatment to help you move better, while addressing what is driving the pain. Relying on a Tens machine for lasting relief Some people swear by transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (Tens) machines, which send mild electrical currents through the body, for pain relief. The signals are designed to travel down nerve pathways to block pain signals from reaching the spinal cord and brain, and to trigger the release of natural painkilling endorphins. The scientific evidence for them is weak, and a systematic review for the World Health Organisation found they produced only brief, marginal reductions in pain. Dr Wood says there may be a place for them, though. “Some people get good relief, particularly if they have a lot of muscle spasm or tension,” she says. “It can calm down the spasms and help the muscles relax.” She says that if you find Tens beneficial, “it’s not going to do you any harm”. But it’s best to think of it as a tool to help you get back to moving more comfortably, rather than something that will fix the underlying issue. Being afraid to bend, lift or exercise The instinct to protect a painful back can be overwhelming, but research shows that this fear can negatively impact the way we move, potentially worsening the problem in the long term. One review published in the journal Physical Therapy found that people with greater fear of movement tended to move their spines through a smaller range when bending. This isn’t what we want, says Dr Wood. “The key message for people with acute pain is try to keep living your life as you normally would,” she says. Movement has several benefits, helping to release spasms and restore the back’s normal range of motion, keeping the joints healthy. So, as long as it’s not causing serious or sharp pain, try to continue to bend down to tie your shoelaces or carry a bag of shopping. But if you’re struggling, Dr Wood advises modifying certain activities, bending more slowly, reducing the weight you’re carrying or breaking the task into smaller chunks. Kate Rowe-Ham, a personal trainer and author of The Longevity Solution, suggests dialing down your exercise regime initially and gently building it back up. “If you have been lifting heavy weights, for instance, use your bodyweight instead,” she says. “Focus on controlled movement and good technique.” And don’t assume every twinge means you’re causing damage. “Hurt does not always equal harm,” she says. Not strengthening your back once the pain has settled Once the initial wave of acute pain has eased, building strength can make your back more resilient. “Working on the core, glutes and the muscles that support the spine will help you to recover fully, and also help prevent the problem recurring,” says Rowe-Ham. She recommends the following simple, controlled exercises: Dead bug Lying on your back with your arms and legs raised, slowly lower the opposite arm and leg towards the floor, keeping your core engaged. Bird dog From all fours, extend one arm and the opposite leg, keeping your hips and shoulders steady. Squats Stand with your feet hip-width apart, bend your knees and push your hips back as if you’re sitting into a chair, then drive through your feet to stand. Single-leg Romanian deadlifts Stand on one leg, soften your knee and slowly hinge forward from the hips, extending the other leg behind you. Keep your back flat and hips level, then squeeze your glutes to return to standing. The ‘happy baby’ stretch Lie on your back, bring your knees towards your chest and hold the insides of your feet.
